subject: physics_2
question_text: What are beats? When do they occur? Explain their use, if any.

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers, so neither check was run. Physics hand-checked: beats need two waves of NEARLY equal frequencies in the same direction; maxima arrive where the waves meet in phase and minima in opposite phase; the beat frequency equals the difference n₁ − n₂ (the book writes n₁ ~ n₂, the positive difference). The book spells 'waining' — corrected to waning throughout.

recall_prompt: Say what beats are, when they occur, the beat frequency formula, and two uses.

steps.label: Definition of beats
lines: When two sound waves of nearly equal
frequencies travel in the same direction
and superpose, the loudness of the sound
rises and falls at regular intervals of
time. This phenomenon is called beats.
steps.margin_note: First mark. The condition — NEARLY equal frequencies — is part of the definition.
steps.why: Nearly equal is the whole condition: equal frequencies give a steady loudness, and widely different frequencies rise and fall too fast for the ear to follow. Only a small difference produces countable beats.
common_mistakes: Writing equal frequencies — equal frequencies give NO beats; the frequencies must be nearly equal.
Leaving out same direction — beats come from superposition along the same line of travel.

recall.must_convey: That beats are the regular rise and fall of loudness when two waves of nearly equal frequencies superpose.
accept: loudness rises and falls at regular intervals
two waves of nearly equal frequencies
reject: beat frequency is n1 minus n2

steps.memory_tip: Three conditions in one sentence: two waves, nearly equal frequencies, same direction.

steps.label: Waxing and waning
lines: Let the two frequencies be n₁ and n₂
(n₁ > n₂). Where the two waves meet in
the same phase, the intensity of sound is
maximum — waxing. Where they meet in
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Same phase = waxing (loud); opposite phase = waning (soft).
steps.why: The two frequencies drift in and out of step because they are not exactly equal — in phase their displacements add (loud), in opposite phase they cancel (soft), and the cycle repeats at a regular interval.
common_mistakes: Swapping the terms — waxing is the loud instant (same phase), waning the soft one (opposite phase).
Saying the waves stay in one phase relation — the small frequency difference makes the phase relation change continuously.

recall.must_convey: That same-phase meetings give maximum intensity (waxing) and opposite-phase meetings give minimum (waning).
accept: the waves drift in and out of step
reject: the number of waxings per second

steps.memory_tip: Waxing = growing loud, waning = fading soft — the same pair of words used for the moon.

steps.label: Beat frequency
lines: The number of waxings (or wanings) heard
in one second is called the beat
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Define it in words first, then write the difference formula.
steps.why: In one second the higher-frequency wave completes n₁ − n₂ more vibrations than the other, so the pair returns to being in phase n₁ − n₂ times — one loud instant each time. The formula IS that counting argument.
common_mistakes: Writing n₁ + n₂ — the sum is not heard as beats; the ear counts the DIFFERENCE.
Giving a negative beat frequency — take n₁ > n₂, or write the positive difference.

recall.must_convey: That the beat frequency equals the difference of the two frequencies, n₁ − n₂.
accept: the difference of the two frequencies
waxings per second equals the difference
reject: used to detect gases in mines

steps.memory_tip: The faster wave gains one full vibration per beat — so beats per second = the frequency difference.

steps.label: Uses of beats
lines: 1) To detect dangerous gases in mines.
2) To produce special sound effects in
3) To find the unknown frequency of a
note, using a fork of known frequency.
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Three named uses close the answer.
steps.why: Each use is the same measurement: a change in beat count reveals a change in one frequency — air with gas changes a pipe's note against a reference, and an unknown fork's frequency sits a counted number of beats from a known one.
common_mistakes: Naming only one use — the question asks for their use, and listed answers earn with two or three items.

recall.must_convey: That beats detect mine gases, make sound effects in films, and find an unknown frequency.

steps.memory_tip: Mines, movies, music — the three m-words of beat uses.

insider_note: The condition nearly equal in the first sentence and the difference formula n₁ − n₂ are the two places this answer usually leaks marks.
